sections.title: The Lord's Vengeance and Redemption
observations: This section begins with a vivid portrayal of the Lord coming from Edom, symbolizing judgment against His enemies. The imagery of stained garments suggests the bloodshed associated with divine retribution.
The question arises: Why does the Lord come from Edom? Edom represents those who oppose God and His people, and this emphasizes God's sovereignty over all nations.
The Lord's declaration of His own power and the mention of His 'day of vengeance' highlight the seriousness of divine justice.

sections.title: The Lord's Compassion and Mercy
observations: In contrast to the previous section, this part reflects on God's compassion for His people. Despite their rebellion, He remembers His covenant and acts to save them.
The imagery of God bearing their burdens and saving them illustrates His deep love and commitment to His people, even in their unfaithfulness.
This section emphasizes the dual nature of God as both a just judge and a merciful savior.

sections.title: A Plea for Deliverance
observations: The chapter concludes with a heartfelt plea from the people, recalling God's past mercies and asking for His intervention in their current suffering.
This plea reflects a deep understanding of their need for God's grace and a recognition of their own failures.
The mention of the Holy Spirit's role in guiding and leading them underscores the importance of divine presence in their lives.

importantVerses.commentary: Who is this coming from Edom, in crimson garments from Bozrah? This one who is splendid in his apparel, marching in the greatness of his strength? It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save!

I will recount the steadfast love of the Lord, the praises of the Lord, according to all that the Lord has granted us, and the great goodness to the house of Israel that he has granted them according to his compassion, according to the abundance of his steadfast love.
We have become like those over whom you have never ruled, like those who are not called by your name.

questions: What does the imagery of the Lord coming from Edom signify for the nations and for Israel?
How do God's justice and mercy coexist in this chapter?
What can we learn from the people's plea for deliverance in relation to our own prayers and understanding of God's character?
